questions.q: Why does Daniel plan his study time differently?
choices: He wants a longer school day.
He needs to help his sister.
His old routine left him tired.
He has already finished every subject.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 provides the evidence for this interpretation. Review the relevant statement and how the other options conflict with it.

questions.q: Why does Daniel check his notes after speaking to his sister?
choices: He has forgotten where she lives.
He cannot explain an idea clearly.
She asks him to study history.
His phone is sending messages.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 provides the evidence for this interpretation. Review the relevant statement and how the other options conflict with it.

questions.q: What does Daniel do before checking the answers to Wednesday's questions?
choices: He writes a new textbook.
He calls his teacher.
He takes the science test.
He tries to answer on his own.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 provides the evidence for this interpretation. Review the relevant statement and how the other options conflict with it.

questions.q: Why does Daniel turn off phone notifications?
choices: To help himself concentrate.
To save the phone battery.
To stop his sister calling.
To make his notes shorter.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 provides the evidence for this interpretation. Review the relevant statement and how the other options conflict with it.

questions.q: Why is Daniel pleased after the test, although he still made mistakes?
choices: The questions were very easy.
He received a perfect result.
His new routine made him calmer.
He did not need to study.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 provides the evidence for this interpretation. Review the relevant statement and how the other options conflict with it.

questions.q: What does Daniel plan to do with his study routine next week?
choices: Stop using it for science.
Try it for history and change it if needed.
Study every subject in one night.
Ask his sister to make every decision.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 provides the evidence for this interpretation. Review the relevant statement and how the other options conflict with it.

questions.q: A student can read notes but cannot explain an idea. What might help?
choices: Ask someone else to take the test.
Read the notes once and stop.
Switch to a different subject forever.
Look again at the difficult part.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 provides the evidence for this interpretation. Review the relevant statement and how the other options conflict with it.

questions.q: Your friend studies all night before a test and feels tired. What could Daniel suggest?
choices: Make a plan with shorter study times.
Stop taking tests at school.
Study for three hours without a break.
Never revise anything on Monday.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 provides the evidence for this interpretation. Review the relevant statement and how the other options conflict with it.

questions.q: Why does the text suggest that a study plan does not have to be perfect?
choices: Mistakes mean nobody should study.
A plan only works for easy subjects.
A useful plan can still be changed.
Good plans always give perfect grades.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 provides the evidence for this interpretation. Review the relevant statement and how the other options conflict with it.

questions.q: After a difficult test, what is a sensible next step?
choices: Throw away all the notes.
Write down what needs more practice.
Study the same way without thinking.
Forget about the next subject.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 provides the evidence for this interpretation. Review the relevant statement and how the other options conflict with it.
